title: The Stuff You Should Know Doin’ Science Playlist: Can Nuclear Fusion Reactors Save The World?
summary: Stuff You Should Know Doin' Science playlist rerun episode on nuclear fusion reactors as a possible energy solution. Josh and Chuck cover the ITER project in Cadarache, France, and its cost and delays; how fusion differs from fission; the Sun as a model; plasma; the history from Lyman Spitzer's stellarator through the Soviet tokamak; deuterium-tritium and deuterium-deuterium fuels, tritium and helium supply; radioactive waste; magnetic versus inertial confinement including the NIF laser facility; Lockheed Martin's compact fusion claim; cold fusion history; international funding; and a listener mail about skywriting in Australia. A Kiva team shout-out is included.
rerun_of: Can Nuclear Fusion Reactors Save The World?

segments.title: Cold open and ITER recommendation
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode, recommends the New Yorker article 'Star in a Bottle' about the ITER fusion reactor in Europe, and notes its delayed start date.

segments.title: Opening banter and ITER overview
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter, then describe ITER in Cadarache, France, its acronym, its roughly fifty billion dollar cost, and its delayed schedule.

segments.title: Promise of fusion energy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why fusion matters: low radioactivity, abundant fuel, no greenhouse emissions, and reuse of existing grid infrastructure. They compare energy yield per kilogram of fuel with fission and coal.

segments.title: The Sun as a model and Taylor Wilson
segments.summary: The hosts explain that stars are natural fusion reactors and that the Sun fuses hydrogen every second. They mention Taylor Wilson, a teenager who built a small fusion device at home.

segments.title: Net energy gain challenge
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the two main challenges: containment material science and achieving net energy gain. They note that ITER's current output is around ten megawatts, with a projected five hundred megawatts once operational.

segments.title: History: Spitzer, stellarator, and the Soviet tokamak
segments.summary: The hosts trace fusion history to Lyman Spitzer's 1950s work and his figure-eight stellarator. They describe how the US and Soviets shared research and how the Soviet tokamak donut design using electromagnets became standard.

segments.title: What plasma is and why temperature matters
segments.summary: Josh explains plasma as a fourth state of matter in which electrons are stripped from atoms. The hosts note the Sun's gravity and explain that Earth must reach higher temperatures, about six times the Sun's core, to compensate for lower density.

segments.title: How fusion and fission release energy
segments.summary: Josh explains fission versus fusion, the electromagnetic repulsion between protons, the strong nuclear force, and mass-energy conversion. He describes how released neutrons carry energy into a blanket that heats water to drive a turbine.

segments.title: Fusion fuels: deuterium, tritium, and helium
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the deuterium-tritium reaction, tritium's radioactivity and lithium sourcing, and deuterium from seawater. They discuss isotopes of hydrogen and a possible helium shortage.

segments.title: Radioactive waste and safety
segments.summary: The hosts explain that fusion produces less long-lived radioactive waste than fission, mainly from activated structural materials, and that fusion cannot melt down like a fission reactor.

segments.title: Magnetic confinement and the ITER design
segments.summary: The hosts explain magnetic confinement in a donut-shaped chamber with electromagnetic rings, the power needed to start a reaction, and the ITER target output. They also describe Lockheed Martin's claimed compact reactor and its scientific skepticism.

segments.title: Lockheed Martin claim and stellarator skepticism
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Lockheed Martin Skunk Works claim, low beta ratio, lack of released data, and the stellarator figure-eight configuration with mirrors that try to contain escaping plasma. They note scientific skepticism.

segments.title: Inertial confinement and NIF lasers
segments.summary: Chuck describes inertial confinement at the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore, where 192 lasers compress a fuel pellet inside a target chamber. Josh and Chuck discuss how it avoids the need for electromagnets.

segments.title: Cold fusion history and international funding
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1989 cold fusion claims with palladium, failed replication, and a 2005 UCLA pyroelectric fusion result with negative net energy. They then discuss funding for ITER from the EU, South Korea, China, the US, and Russia.

segments.title: Wrap-up and DIY fusion
segments.summary: Josh recommends the New Yorker article. Chuck mentions instructables for home fusion projects and notes that Taylor Wilson's device was legitimate.

segments.title: Kiva team shout-out
segments.summary: The hosts promote the stuff you should know Kiva lending team, reporting its loan totals and encouraging listeners to join.

segments.title: Listener mail: skywriting from Australia
segments.summary: A listener from Sydney, Australia recounts watching a plane skywrite the word Hooters backwards as a child, and the hosts discuss the backwards writing.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give contact and website information.
